title: Tier IV Checkpoint I — A Research-Grounded View

points.h: SLA Theory as a Living Debate
pts: No single acquisition theory has won outright — Input, Interaction, and Output Hypotheses remain in productive, ongoing tension.
This series' own practical guidance has drawn compatibly on all three throughout, reflecting genuine theoretical pluralism.
Holding this uncertainty comfortably, rather than needing false certainty, is itself a mark of theoretical maturity.

v: A lesson plan from Unit 10 or Unit 35; three coloured pens

items: Distribute a complete lesson plan from earlier in the book.
Participants mark each stage in three colours: input (reading, listening), interaction (pair talk, negotiation) and output (speaking, writing).
For each stage, note which hypothesis from Unit 77 best explains its value.
Identify any stage that no theory clearly supports.
Discuss: does the lesson need all three? Could it work with only one?
Participants mark their own lesson plan from the past week.
Support: provide a short summary card of each hypothesis.
Challenge: add a fourth colour for sociocultural concepts such as scaffolding.

blocks.x: One group’s notes on a lesson about train journeys:

lines: Listening to a station announcement: input (comprehensible, with a clear purpose).
Pairs completing an information gap: interaction (negotiation of meaning).
Role-play at the ticket counter: output (pushed to be accurate and polite).
A: So the lesson already uses all three theories without naming them.
B: And if we cut the role-play for time, we lose the output.

blocks.x: Holding the three theories together, rather than choosing one, is what Unit 77 called productive tension.

body: Purpose: to show a lesson supported by several theories. Content: a lesson plan page with stages highlighted in three colours and a small legend (input, interaction, output); the colours overlap in some stages. Style: realistic document with clear labels as well as colours. Board version: a list of stages with I, Int and O beside each.

items: Google Docs (free) with highlighting for shared annotation.

blocks.x: Photocopied lesson plan and coloured pencils.

pts: World Englishes and ELF research establish that no single variety holds automatic linguistic authority over others.
This grounds the critical-language-awareness thread running from Tier III through the remainder of Tier IV.
Practical teaching choices about variety should be informed, deliberate ones, not unexamined defaults.

v: A list of ten Indian English features; a list of classroom materials

items: List ten features of Indian English, such as prepone, do the needful, I am having a cold, or the use of itself for emphasis.
For each, decide: accept in speaking? accept in writing? model? teach as an alternative?
Justify each decision with reference to learners’ needs, intelligibility and the context of use.
Compare decisions across colleagues and note where they differ.
Write a short department statement on varieties of English.
Include features of other varieties learners may meet, such as British, American or Singapore English.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: prepone: accept in speaking and in local writing; point out that international readers may not know it.
I am having a cold: accept in speaking; model I have a cold for formal writing and exams.
do the needful: discuss as a formula; model alternatives for international correspondence.

blocks.x: The decision is informed and deliberate, not a default (Unit 78). Kachru (1985) and later World Englishes research establish that no single variety holds automatic authority, while learners still need to know the conventions their audiences expect.

body: Purpose: to show variety choices as deliberate. Content: a table with features in rows and columns for ‘accept’, ‘model’ and ‘discuss’, with ticks; small flags are avoided in favour of neutral icons. Style: tidy chart. Board version: a four-column table.

items: Google Sheets (free) for a shared decision table.

blocks.x: A chart in the staff room.

pts: The gap between stated belief and actual practice, and the deep roots of teacher cognition, explain much of the real-world variation in how identical training gets implemented.
This connects to this series' own aim throughout — reasoned explanation over bare prescription, precisely to shape genuine belief, not just surface compliance.
Reflective examination of one's own cognition remains the most reliable lever for genuine practice change.

v: Belief statements from Unit 79; a recording or notes from one lesson

items: Re-read the belief statements you wrote in Unit 79.
Watch a recording of one of your own lessons, or review a colleague’s observation notes.
Note moments where practice matched belief and where it did not.
For each gap, identify a reason: time, exam pressure, class size, habit or a belief you had not noticed.
Choose one gap to work on and plan a small change.
Pair with a mentor (Unit 68) for a joint review.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A teacher’s notes (written for this book):

lines: Belief: Learners learn best by speaking.
Practice: I talked for 28 of 40 minutes.
Reason: fear of noise; the head teacher’s room is next door.
Change: two-minute whispered pair tasks, with a signal to stop.

blocks.x: Borg (2003) describes the complex relationship between teachers’ beliefs and practices. Examining one’s own cognition in this way remains one of the most reliable routes to lasting change.

body: Purpose: to show the gap between belief and practice. Content: a teacher with a speech bubble reading ‘learners should talk’ standing at the front of a class, talking; a second scene shows the same teacher listening as pairs talk. Style: gentle humour, realistic. Board version: two stick figures with speech bubbles.

items: A phone’s video or audio recorder for self-observation (with school permission).

blocks.x: A colleague’s observation notes on a simple timeline sheet.

body: Research on teacher cognition has found that teachers’ own experiences as learners, often called the apprenticeship of observation, can shape their teaching long after training ends. The phrase comes from the sociologist Dan Lortie’s study Schoolteacher (1975) [VERIFY edition].

points.h: Materials Design Rests on Real Evidence
pts: The practical materials-writing craft from Tier III rests on a genuine, if imperfect and still-developing, research base.
Authenticity's benefits are more contested than commonly assumed — a useful corrective to unexamined assumption.
This evidence should inform, without rigidly dictating, the practical judgement materials writing still requires.

v: One unit of self-written materials (Unit 69); Tomlinson’s principles (Unit 80)

items: Take a unit of materials you have written.
List the principles behind each activity (for example, affective engagement, noticing, meaningful output).
For each principle, rate the strength of evidence: strong, some, or mainly professional judgement.
Discuss the contested case of authenticity: when are authentic texts helpful, and when are adapted texts better?
Revise one activity in the light of the discussion.
Evaluate a coursebook unit in the same way.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Activity: reading a real bus timetable. Principle: authenticity. Evidence: some; benefits depend on level and task.
Activity: pre-reading prediction. Principle: activating schemata. Evidence: some.
Activity: personal response to a poem. Principle: affective engagement. Evidence: mainly professional judgement and learner feedback.

blocks.x: Tomlinson (2011) presents principles that combine research findings with experience. Evidence should inform the choice, but practical judgement still decides.

body: Purpose: to show materials design as a balance. Content: a balance scale with ‘research evidence’ on one side and ‘teacher judgement’ on the other, a worksheet resting on the beam. Style: clean, symbolic. Board version: a simple scale with two labels.

items: Google Docs (free) for comment-based evaluation of materials.

blocks.x: A printed evaluation sheet with three columns.

pts: Understanding research methods equips genuinely critical engagement with claims — including many made throughout this very series.
Sample size, methodology, and replication status all affect how much confidence a given finding actually deserves.
This critical stance is a permanent professional tool, not a one-time poster's content.

v: Five claims from earlier units; the checklist from Unit 81

items: Choose five research-based claims from different units of this book.
Apply the three questions from Unit 81: what was measured, who and how many, and does the claim fit the data?
Trace at least one claim to its original source.
Rate the confidence each claim deserves, and note any need for a more cautious wording.
Discuss how critical reading applies to all sources, including trusted ones.
Apply the same process to a state training module or a popular teacher blog.
Support: provide the original abstracts.
Challenge: participants look for meta-analyses or replications relevant to each claim.

blocks.x: A trainee’s notes (written for this book):

lines: Claim from Unit 8: corrective feedback can help learning. Source: meta-analyses such as Lyster and Saito (2010). Confidence: fairly high for oral feedback in the studies included; less known for large classes in India.
Claim from Unit 31: extensive reading supports vocabulary and fluency. Confidence: reasonable, with many studies; effects vary with time spent.
A: Should we trust the book less now?
B: We should trust it the right amount.

body: Purpose: to show critical reading applied to this book. Content: a reader holding this book with a magnifying glass over a page; margin notes read ‘source?’, ‘sample?’ and ‘fits the data?’. Style: friendly, slightly playful. Board version: a book outline with three question marks.

items: Google Scholar (free) to trace sources.

blocks.x: The printed book and the reference list at the end of each unit.

body: When you teach a theory or cite research in training, say how strong the evidence is. ‘Several large studies agree’ and ‘one small study suggests’ are both honest, and trainees learn to calibrate by hearing you do it.

pts: Cognitive linguistics and sociocultural theory each offer genuine, complementary insight beyond the Chomskyan and behaviourist traditions referenced earlier in this series.
Neither displaces the other — both illuminate different dimensions of a genuinely complex phenomenon.
This reinforces, once again, this series' consistent stance of principled theoretical pluralism over singular orthodoxy.

v: Technique cards; summary cards for Units 82 and 83

items: Give groups one technique each, such as teaching phrasal verbs, peer feedback or a grammar timeline.
Groups explain the technique first in cognitive-linguistic terms and then in sociocultural terms.
Groups decide which lens offers the stronger explanation for this technique.
Groups present one technique that both lenses explain well.
Discuss how multiple theories can coexist in a teacher’s thinking.
Add the Chomskyan and behaviourist traditions mentioned earlier in the book.
Support: provide key terms from each framework.
Challenge: identify a technique that neither lens explains.

lines: Phrasal verbs taught through up and out: cognitive lens strong (particle meaning); sociocultural lens weaker, unless learners explain meanings to each other.
Peer feedback: sociocultural lens strong (mediation, collaboration); cognitive lens weaker.
A timeline drawn together by a pair: both. The drawing is a cognitive representation of meaning, and the talk around it is mediation.

blocks.x: Neither lens displaces the other. Each illuminates a different dimension of learning, which is the principled pluralism argued for in Units 25 and 77.

body: Purpose: to show complementary frameworks. Content: two overlapping circles, one labelled ‘cognitive’ (with a timeline icon) and one ‘sociocultural’ (with two speech bubbles); techniques placed in each circle and in the overlap. Style: clear Venn diagram. Board version: two overlapping circles with words.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for a printable diagram.

blocks.x: A Venn diagram on chart paper with sticky notes.

pts: AI's impact on ELT is real, current, and still unfolding — this poster's content will likely need updating faster than most of this series.
This is itself an important lesson: expert practice includes staying current, not treating any single snapshot of the field as final.
This connects to Unit 67's action-research habit, applied to tracking a genuinely fast-moving area of change.

items: List three areas that are changing quickly, such as AI tools (Unit 84), assessment policy and digital platforms.
Choose one reliable source for each (a journal, a government portal, a professional association).
Each month, note one development and its possible effect on your teaching.
Every term, try one change in class and evaluate it with a small action-research cycle (Unit 67).
Share the log at cluster or DIET meetings.
A group of teachers divides the areas and reports to each other.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A log entry (written for this book):

lines: Month: August. Area: AI tools. Development: a free app now offers speaking practice in English with feedback. Possible effect: home practice for learners with phones. Action: trial with volunteers for four weeks; survey at the end.

blocks.x: Staying current does not mean adopting everything. It means knowing what is changing and testing it where it matters.

body: Purpose: to show staying current as a routine. Content: a calendar page with small notes for each month and a lightbulb for the month in which a change was tried. Style: tidy, practical. Board version: a grid of twelve boxes with a few ticks.

items: Feedly (free plan) or email alerts from Google Scholar (free) to follow new research.
Professional associations such as ELTAI (English Language Teachers’ Association of India) for newsletters and events [VERIFY membership terms].

blocks.x: A notebook log and printed newsletters shared at meetings.

pts: Every theoretical thread in this stretch connects directly back to specific, concrete practices from earlier in this series.
This is the central claim of Tier IV: theory doesn't replace practice, it deepens and justifies the understanding beneath it.
The next stretch of this tier extends this same theory-practice connection into acquisition, bilingualism, and teacher training.

v: Unit titles 76–84 on cards; unit titles 1–75 on a list

items: Give each group two theory units from Units 76–84.
Groups find at least three practical units from Parts I–III that each theory explains or justifies.
Groups prepare a one-minute explanation for each connection.
Build a class map linking theory units to practice units.
Each participant writes a short rationale for one lesson they will teach next week, naming the theory behind each stage.
Use the map as the basis for a DIET training module.
Support: provide a partly completed map.
Challenge: participants identify a practice unit that no theory yet covers and suggest which later unit (86–99) might.

lines: Unit 83 (sociocultural theory) → Unit 15 (scaffolding), Unit 34 (cooperative learning), Unit 43 (peer feedback).
Unit 82 (cognitive linguistics) → Unit 5 (chunks), Unit 6 (grammar in context), Unit 58 (corpus).
Unit 81 (research methods) → Unit 67 (action research), Unit 9 (reflective planning).
T: What does this map tell you?
S1: That nothing we did earlier was only a trick. Each technique has a reason.
T: And the reason tells you when to change it.

body: Purpose: to show theory and practice connected. Content: two rows of labelled circles, theory units above and practice units below, joined by lines; at the centre, a teacher with a lesson plan. Style: clean network diagram. Board version: two rows of numbers joined by lines.

items: Miro (free plan, limited boards) for a digital concept map.

blocks.x: Unit cards and string on a wall.

body: For one lesson next week, write a single sentence beside each stage of your plan naming the theory that justifies it. Afterwards, note one stage where the theory helped you adjust in the moment.

dek: Unit 85 of 100: closing the opening stretch of Tier IV by synthesising the theoretical landscape Units 76 through 84 have built, into one coherent picture.

aims.x: This checkpoint closes the first stretch of Part IV. Units 76 to 84 have moved through SLA theory, World Englishes, teacher cognition, materials design, research methods, cognitive linguistics, sociocultural theory and artificial intelligence. Each unit could be read on its own. This unit asks what they add up to, and how theory can return to the classroom as better-reasoned practice. Its activities are designed mainly for teachers, teacher educators and DIET faculty, and several can be run as a single half-day workshop.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain why competing SLA theories can each inform practice without any one of them being final;
make informed, deliberate choices about the varieties of English you model and accept;
examine your own teaching beliefs and the gaps between belief and practice;
use research evidence to inform, without dictating, materials decisions;
apply critical reading habits to research claims, including those in this book;
use cognitive and sociocultural lenses together to explain classroom techniques;
plan a way of staying current in a fast-changing field;
connect each theoretical thread in Units 76–84 to specific practices from earlier in the book.

why: Why this matters. Nine posters of theory only prove their value when they connect back to practice. This checkpoint draws that connection explicitly before the tier continues.

background.x: Part IV began with a claim in Unit 76: that theory does not replace practice but deepens the understanding beneath it. Since then, the units have shown a field in which no single account has won. Krashen’s input hypothesis, Long’s interaction hypothesis and Swain’s output hypothesis (Unit 77) each capture something real; cognitive linguistics (Unit 82) and sociocultural theory (Unit 83) offer different starting points again. Surveys of the field present these as partly complementary lenses on a complex phenomenon (Lightbown and Spada 2013; Ellis 2008). Unit 86 will return to Universal Grammar and the acquisition debates in more depth.

At the same time, Units 78 and 79 turned attention to people. The spread of English has created many Englishes, described in Braj Kachru’s model of Inner, Outer and Expanding Circles (Kachru 1985), and research on English as a lingua franca has questioned whether any single native-speaker norm should be the target for every learner (Jenkins 2007). Research on teacher cognition shows that what teachers believe, know and think shapes how they interpret any theory or training (Borg 2003). Units 80 and 81 then turned to evidence itself: the research base for materials design (Tomlinson 2011) and the methods by which research claims are made and should be read.

For Indian teachers and teacher educators, this is not an abstract exercise. B. Kumaravadivelu (2006) argued that teachers should build their own theory of practice, sensitive to local particularity, rather than applying imported methods, and N. S. Prabhu’s idea of a teacher’s sense of plausibility (Unit 25) points in the same direction. NEP 2020 and NCF 2023 both ask teachers to make informed pedagogical choices, to use home languages as resources and to engage in continuous professional development (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). A DIET lecturer preparing a training module, or a teacher planning a term, needs exactly this capacity: to know why a technique works, when it might not, and how to find out.

The activities below each revisit one unit and connect it back to practice. Together they form a checkpoint: a chance to consolidate before Part IV continues with acquisition, bilingualism and teacher education.

items: Annotated lesson. A lesson plan annotated with input, interaction, output, cognitive and sociocultural rationales.
Variety statement. A department statement on varieties of English, with reasons for each decision.
Belief–practice review. A short reflective account of one gap between belief and practice and the change planned.
Theory–practice map. A map linking Units 76–84 to specific practices, with brief explanations.
Which theory from Units 76–84 has most changed how you see your teaching?
Which of your classroom decisions are still defaults rather than deliberate choices?
How comfortable are you with uncertainty in theory? How do you explain it to trainees?
How do you decide which research claims to trust?
How will you stay current without being overwhelmed?
What would you like the rest of Part IV to explain?

Kumaravadivelu, B. 2006. Understanding Language Teaching: From Method to Postmethod. Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum.

Screenshots of Google Docs, Google Sheets, Miro, Canva, Feedly or Google Scholar require permission or replacement with original illustrations. terms.def: Lortie’s (1975) term for the many hours future teachers spend watching their own teachers as pupils, which shapes their beliefs about teaching before any training begins.

Matching the confidence of a claim to the strength of the research behind it, for example ‘several large studies agree’ versus ‘one small study suggests’. Teacher educators model it when they cite research.

An approach to teaching based on the postmethod condition and the parameters of particularity, practicality and possibility, which positions teachers as theorizers of their own practice (Kumaravadivelu 2001).
Holding several theories together in planning and teaching, rather than choosing one, so that their differences lead to a richer, more balanced practice.

A teacher’s own developing understanding of how learning happens, which guides classroom decisions (Prabhu 1990). Prabhu argued it matters more than any one method, and that it stays alive through reflection and engagement with ideas.
What teachers know, believe and think, and how this relates to what they do in the classroom (Borg 2003). It is shaped by schooling, training, experience and context.

Recognizing that several theories, such as cognitive, sociocultural and usage-based accounts, each explain part of language learning, and drawing on them thoughtfully rather than committing to only one.

The relationship between theories of language learning and teachers’ classroom decisions. Teachers make the link by testing ideas against their experience and by using theory to explain what they observe.

The varieties of English used around the world, such as Indian, Nigerian and Singaporean English, each seen as legitimate with its own norms. The concept is closely associated with Kachru’s Three Circles model.
